consensus_summary: Across the blind responses, the settled primary meaning of “life”/“the life” (esp. zōē) is eternal/divine life given through Christ, with “the Life” also functioning as a christological title for Christ himself as its source and embodiment; covenantal, physical, resurrection, and Spirit-related senses appear only as secondary alternatives.
book_summary: The book defines “Life (the life)” as covenant existence—the life lived by walking in the Way according to God’s law—while explicitly noting that the common teaching is instead Christ himself and the eternal life imparted to believers.
consensus_core_identification: eternal/divine life in or through Christ (or Christ himself as “the Life”)
book_core_identification: covenant existence (life lived walking in the Way according to God’s law)
boundary_disagreement: The book demotes the christological/eternal-life identification (consensus primary) to a mere “commonly taught” view and elevates the Deuteronomic/covenantal-obedience sense (consensus secondary alternative) to the sole definitional core, thereby excluding Christ-as-Life and imparted zōē as the proper referent of the term.
material_contradiction: Consensus identifies the referent as Christ or the eternal life he is/gives; the book identifies it as the believer’s law-observant walk. These cannot both be the primary symbolic identification of the same term in the same sense.
rationale: Minimum cores are non-equivalent: one is a person/gift (Christ/eternal life), the other a mode of covenantal conduct. The book’s own common-view note marks the separation. Although a covenantal reading appears among consensus alternatives, elevating it while displacing the christological core constitutes replacement, not refinement or narrowing of the same referent. Citation overlap (esp. John 14:6) does not erase the divergent identification.
strongest_objection: John 14:6 and the dominant Johannine/NT usage treat “the life” as a title of Christ himself, so the book’s reduction to covenant-law walking under-reads the very texts it cites.
